 Coach O survives sepsis after innovative diagnostic test 
 Coach Ed Orgeron (FMOL Health) By Raley Pellittieri Published : Nov. 12, 2026 at 2:48 PM CST Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - Coach Ed Orgeron is back on the sidelines as LSU Football’s special assistant for recruiting and defense, but he started the football season off fighting for his life. 
 According to FMOL Health, Orgeron was rushed to Our Lady of the Lake Regional Medical Center in August after an infection in his leg turned into sepsis, a life-threatening condition that can overtake the body in hours. 
 If left untreated, health officials say sepsis can permanently damage organs and ultimately cause death. 
 Doctors credited an innovative, first-of-its-kind diagnostic test with saving the national championship-winning coach’s life. It was researched and developed by LSU, Our Lady of the Lake, and biotech company Cytovale. 
 According to the Source , a blog published by FMOL Health, Orgeron’s blood pressure had fallen to 60/40 by the time he reached the emergency department. 
 FMOL Health said the IntelliSep test immediately detected sepsis, and life-saving treatment started. 
 The Source said Orgeron spent seven days in the intensive care unit, and later left the hospital 28 pounds heavier from fluid, with a swollen leg and a long road ahead. 
 Dr. Hollis “Bud” O’Neal, one of the physicians who cared for Orgeron at Our Lady of the Lake, was the lead researcher responsible for developing the innovative test that helped save Orgeron’s life. 
 IntelliSep analyzes the response of white blood cells from a standard blood sample and provides results in under 10 minutes to help clinicians assess the probability of sepsis, FMOL Health explained. 
 “With sepsis, early recognition saves time and lives, and through the IntelliSep test we were able to immediately determine that Coach was septic and in need of life-saving measures,” O’Neal said. “Our Lady of the Lake was the first hospital in the nation to develop and implement a test like this. If you think about it, Coach O was at the exact right place, our hospital, at the exact right time, to ensure he made it through.” 
 The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that at least 1.7 million adults in the U.S. develop sepsis annually, and at least 350,000 die as a result.
